tags.gist: A psychiatry resident says the framework does not capture GenAI risk, wants clear warnings on any medical guidance, and prefers human mental health care.
Repeats that any output carrying medical guidance needs a clear message and that people should keep relying on human mental health professionals.
Wants every clinic and user to carry a disclaimer that AI is not fail-safe and results may vary, with behavioral health facilities ensuring patient safety.
Repeats that patients should keep relying on human professionals rather than AI models in the mental health field.
Wants every form of AI output translated into different languages and broken down for patients.
Says AI is more work than help, no safeguard can mitigate the risk, and only keeping humans in place fixes it.
Describes a clinical AI tool flagging out-of-scope questions but doubts that stops misuse elsewhere, and has stopped using it.
Says there are no acceptable trade-offs in any clinical context and that AI currently carries more risk and responsibility than it is worth.
Finds the approach ideal on its face but asks how patient data would be kept safe during it and who would answer for leaks.
Says the two-axis framework is unnecessary and asks how patient data will be protected from breach, theft or sale.
Calls the benchmarking structure nice but wants a clinical trial or study with informed consent and safeguards for confidentiality.
Has no answer but says the benchmark needs fleshing out through a pilot and a behavioral health study, asking who is responsible for consent.
Rejects skipping prospective studies: run a clinical trial and be open about it with everyone, including the public.
Suggests survey studies and checking accuracy of information and patient data, while calling informed consent dicey.
Says almost every group, especially behavioral health, elderly, children, non-English and rural patients, is hard to cover, so limited studies give limited data.
Doubts a clinician-panel comparator makes sense, since few physicians would agree to take part for fear of backlash and risk to their license.
Finds the question unanswerable without a pilot, rejects unaided judgment and delayed specialist review as comparators, and doubts a robot can justify no intervention.
Welcomes an independent third party and wants research boards, NIH, NAMI, SAMHSA and the AMA involved, while doubting it is possible.
Likes the competency approach but wants FDA to gather public opinion first from many groups, with a plain-language paper.
